| E115 | Mechanism of the E111 release failure: the maintenance owner is a shared-custody child, and the bank releases only on the LAST child | The typing `detachReturned173` gate is satisfied at the final attempt (`producerReturned=true`, `transferred=true`, `caller` acknowledged, `consumer` present, `original`/`marker` clear), yet the asserted drop does not happen. Both consumers in that class (`actualAppRejectThrowAndPressurePreserveOneCompleteConsumerWithoutProducerReplay173c` and `actualCallerBorrowAndIndependentOldSiblingPreventFullDataRefund173c`) fail, consistent with a custody that never empties. The maintenance owner is derived from the generation's owned descriptor (`servicePackage` → `ownedDescriptor81` → `captureExecutionPin`/`capturedRecord`, `javascript_plugin_host.cj:826-835,2121-2126`), and each distinct `OwnedPluginPackageDescriptor` brings its own payment/backing (`agent_plugin_registry/src/registry_owned_metadata.cj:48-58,194`), so the chain is per-descriptor and the release rule above is what decides whether the bank ever drops. The E111 assertion requires a strict drop after exactly one child acknowledgement, so it can only pass when that child was the custody's last live lease — i.e. the fixture's custody still holds another live lease at that moment. This is a genuine allocation-accounting boundary of the shared-bank work (E91), not a mere label problem, and it cannot be satisfied by loosening the assertion. No production code, assertion, budget or Native input was changed. | `checkpoint_retention_native173.cj:42-53`; `logical_json_payload.cj:152-164,196,247-254`; typing gate verified by probe at `detachReturned173` |

| E118 | Exact per-iteration retention of the bank-pressure loop, attributed to the host handshake payload budgets | From the captured acquisition sequence, each loop iteration permanently adds exactly **33,950,072 bytes**, the same figure E74 recorded, made of one charge of 16,777,216 and one of 17,172,856 (= 16,777,216 + 395,640). | E125 | Behavioural failure behind the contract compile fixes: the safe-cut executor panics on its retained context | With `agent_core_contract` compiling, its own `coreCatalogSafeCutContracts` still fails: `IllegalStateException: contract failed: the already-requested first tool keeps its original executor despite concurrent directory publication` (`catalog_safe_cut.cj:126`). A further probe confirms the context reports `hasOwnedToolSetSnapshot159=false` and `hasOwnedInvocationData180=false` at that point. Both readings change product or contract semantics, so neither was applied mechanically. Resolving it needs a decision on the intended contract rather than a mechanical edit, so no production or test change was made. What this means for the retained-lease hypothesis (E197-E199): a cumulative-resource explanation predicts monotone dependence on the number of prior reads, and this measurement is not monotone - so that hypothesis is WEAKENED but not eliminated, since retention is real and the full sequence does maximize retained leases. | E238 | Incidental observation from cleanup: every `hub_process_read`/`hub_process` invocation left a live broker worker behind, and they outlived the client | Cleaning up after the E235/E236 repro left 208 live `agent_app __process-broker-worker` processes and 48 daemon bash loops, ALL rooted under my `the repro scratch roots` scratch directories (verified: zero non-matching), so I killed precisely those. | E239 | During the hang the client is blocked on an in-process futex, not on the broker or any I/O | Sampled the real CLI process during the hung `wait` (identified by `/proc/<pid>/exe` pointing at `target/release/bin/agent_app` and the cmdline naming the `hub_process_read` wait invocation, because `pgrep -f` otherwise matches the `timeout` wrapper). (a) The stall is a LOCK or CONDITION wait inside the client process, not a network read: a client blocked on an unanswered broker reply would sit in `read`/`poll` on the socket (and the broker's own threads confirmed it answers, E238), whereas here the main thread waits on a futex while the epoll thread is idle. (b) Since a healthy `wait` returns in seconds and uses the same single socket, the difference between the passing and hanging runs is inside the process - which fits the observation that the hang is flaky in the composition of prior calls rather than in any single request (E236). | E240 | Under the debugger the same `wait` does NOT hang - it fails fast with `owner.peer_disconnected`, which relocates the stall to a timing/ordering window | E239 left the hang as an in-process futex wait. Running the identical sequence with the `wait` invocation launched under gdb gave a DIFFERENT outcome: instead of blocking, the client reported `owner peer ended before the next complete frame (owner.peer_disconnected)` and **exited 1 within seconds** with all seven threads cleanly exited. Two readings, and the evidence favours the second. (a) Debugger effect: gdb stops threads at entry, changing scheduling enough to avoid the window - possible, since gdb was started before `run` rather than attached to an already-hung process. (b) More likely: the stall is a race whose two outcomes are mutually exclusive - either the client waits on a futex for a peer frame that never arrives (E239's observation) or it observes the peer as gone and reports `owner.peer_disconnected`. Under gdb (slower startup, detached-after-fork traces) the peer's exit is noticed BEFORE the client enters the wait, so it fails fast; without gdb the client enters the wait first and blocks forever because no reconnect or second frame ever arrives. That makes `owner.peer_disconnected` the proper diagnosis of the stalled case as well: the wait is blocked waiting for a frame from a worker whose peer has already ended, and nothing converts that into an error on the blocking path. It also explains E236's flakiness without any count threshold - the race lands either way depending on when the broker worker exits relative to the client's wait entry. Not yet verified: whether the worker reliably ends at that point, and where the blocking path should surface the disconnect. | gdb run: `owner peer ended before the next complete frame (owner.peer_disconnected)`, `Inferior 1 exited with code 01` in ~60s total; E239 (`futex_do_wait`) and E236 (flaky) |

| E241 | Strongest mechanism candidate for the stall: the peer frame reader retries an idle socket timeout forever | Reading `readWholeFrameHelper180` (`agent_product/src/product_owner_peer180.cj:96-124`) gives a concrete way to block indefinitely, which is what E239 observed and E240's gdb run bypassed. On `SocketTimeoutException` the reader does: `let continueIdle = idle && !closing && bytes.isEmpty()` then **`if (continueIdle) { continue }`** - i.e. as long as the peer is marked `idle`, is not closing, and no partial frame has arrived, a read timeout does not produce `owner.peer_frame_timeout` but silently retries. The only other exit is `count <= 0`, which returns `owner.peer_disconnected` (':116-117', the exact error E240 saw under gdb), or a `SocketException` that is rethrown unless `closing && bytes.isEmpty()`. So the two observed outcomes are both explained by this one function: if the read eventually returns EOF the caller gets `owner.peer_disconnected` promptly (gdb timing), and if it keeps timing out while `idle` stays true the loop never terminates (the un-gdb hang). Two qualifications I will not overstate: the E239 sample put the MAIN thread in `futex_do_wait` rather than in a socket read, so this loop may run on another thread while the main one waits on a lock/'condition' it will never receive, and I have not yet proven that `idle` remains true in the hanging case. The minimal discriminating test is to log `(idle, closing, bytes.isEmpty())` at each timeout, or to check whether forcing `idle=false` converts the hang into `owner.peer_frame_timeout`; both are cheap and neither is done. Recording it as a candidate, not a diagnosis. | `product_owner_peer180.cj:96-124` (`continueIdle` continue at :101-103, `owner.peer_disconnected` returns at :110-117); E239/E240 |

| E242 | The idle-retry is one-way and by design, which moves the defect question to the client's own bound | `idle` is a latch: declared `false` (`product_owner_peer180.cj:35`) and set `true` only by `enableAuthenticatedIdle180()` (`:55`), called once after a successful frontend handshake at `process_broker.cj:422` and once at `:2268`; nothing anywhere sets it back to false. So once a peer is authenticated it is permanently 'idle-eligible', and `readWholeFrameHelper180`'s `if (continueIdle) { continue }` (`:99-103`) means the broker side will keep re-reading rather than fail - which is defensible for a persistent authenticated session, and is therefore probably NOT the bug on its own. What that reframes is where the missing bound lives: the client's `wait` op carries an explicit user-facing `timeout` (3s in my repro) and must return within it, yet E239 observed the client parked on a futex with everything else healthy. So the open question is no longer 'why does the frame reader retry' (answered: by design) but 'which client-side wait ignores its own timeout', and the E240 gdb run shows that when the peer's end IS observed the client exits promptly with `owner.peer_disconnected` - i.e. the error path works, it is simply never taken while the session stays idle-eligible. This narrows the search to the client's wait loop and is the most specific statement this session has produced about the stall. | `product_owner_peer180.cj:35,55,99-103`; `process_broker.cj:422,2268`; E239/E240/E241 |

| E243 | Gate blocker mechanism located: the post-ACK refund requires `transferred`, which only `finishHandoff(true)` sets - so the assertion fails exactly when the consumer was acknowledged without the poll having transferred | E229 recorded that the gate's only remaining failure is `@Expect(nativeControlMetadataUsage113()[1] < beforeAck)` after `acknowledgeAfterConsumption()` (`checkpoint_maintenance_failure173c_test.cj:135`). The refund path is `collectOwnedCheckpointFailure113` -> `collectOwnedFailureAcknowledgements113` -> `if (slot.isConsumed()) { slot.retireMetadata() }` (`application.cj:2651-2668`), and `retireMetadata()` is the only thing that closes the owner (`application_owned_failure113.cj:139-143`). `isConsumed()` requires THREE conditions (`:129-136`): `transferred && !invoking && !handingOff`, plus the published value being acknowledged. `transferred` is set in exactly one place - `finishHandoff(accepted)` with `accepted == true` (`:125-127`) - and `finishHandoff` is called from `admitOwnedCheckpointFailure113` (`application.cj:2515-2533`) with whatever the caller's `accept` callback returned, and from the poll paths at `:2582-2583`/`:2611-2612` where it is hardcoded true. So the assertion fails iff the slot's value was acknowledged while `transferred` stayed false, i.e. the consumer was acknowledged on a path that did not go through a poll that transferred it. That is a coherent, specific condition rather than a mystery, and it also explains why the base and draft versions behave identically (E234): the machinery is unchanged. What is NOT decided is whether the test's sequence should have transferred the slot (test error) or whether the acknowledge-after-consumption path must also mark the handoff accepted (production gap) - both readings remain open, both need an owner decision, and E203 warns against guessing. | `application.cj:2515-2533,2649-2668`; `application_owned_failure113.cj:125-143`; `checkpoint_maintenance_failure173c_test.cj:135`; E229/E234 |

| E246 | E231's conflict is a real incompatibility, now shown to be one of SATURATION METHOD rather than of capacity - which points at the actual fix | Established by reading the reservation paths, not by inference: the host pressure tests that regressed when I widened the App bank use the VERY SAME bank (`reserveNativeDocumentPayload` -> `nativePayloadOwnerBudget.acquire(...)`, `native_payload.cj:210-213`, and `nativeControlMetadataUsage113` is literally `nativePayloadOwnerBudget.usage()`, `:40-43`), so widening it necessarily changed what they observe. | E248 | E246's proposed fix is NOT mechanical: these host cases use a headroom ORACLE calibrated to 128 MiB, so re-expressing them is a redesign | Reading one regressed case exactly (`host_live_policy_session_custody_test.cj:73-96`) shows the mechanism. `liveSessionProbe()` (`:37-39`) reserves 4 MiB - charged `max(16 MiB, 8x)` = 32 MiB - and returns true only if that SUCCEEDS, i.e. it is a 'is there >= 32 MiB headroom?' oracle. Those truth values hold only while the aggregate is small enough that the case's own 64 MiB pressure reservation (`reserveNativeDocumentPayload(8388608)` -> `max(16 MiB, 8x)` = 64 MiB, `native_payload.cj:210-213`) plus the retained custody pushes the bank within 32 MiB of its ceiling. At 512 MiB every oracle reading becomes `true` and the `false` expectations invert. Worse for the mechanical-fix plan: `reserveNativeDocumentPayload` caps at 8 MiB, so its charge cannot exceed 64 MiB and a single case cannot cheaply fill a 512 MiB bank - filling it would take roughly eight such reservations and would change what each case is actually testing. So E246 was right about the mechanism and too optimistic about the cost: making these cases pass at a larger aggregate means redesigning each oracle's calibration, not sweeping a literal. That makes E247's conclusion firmer - the choice between (a) keeping 128 MiB and finding where `goal_contract`'s context-read failure actually comes from, and (b) moving to a larger aggregate and redesigning ~15 host cases, is a maintainer decision. | `host_live_policy_session_custody_test.cj:37-39,73-96`; `native_payload.cj:210-213`; `logical_json_payload.cj:48-54`; E246/E247 |

| E254 | FINAL determination on the bank conflict: E248's 'not mechanical' is now proven arithmetically, and the decision is reduced to a clean two-way choice | E253 proved the App genuinely needs more than 128 MiB for a full session (each observed content query charges at least 16 MiB). But a single reservation is capped twice: `reserveNativeDocumentPayload` rejects `bytes > 8388608` (`native_payload.cj:211`) and `acquire` charges `max(16 MiB, 8 x bytes)` (`logical_json_payload.cj:50-51`), so the largest charge one reservation can add is **64 MiB**. Against a 128 MiB bank that is half the bank - ample to make the oracle fail as intended. Against a 512 MiB bank it is one eighth, so the oracle would report 'headroom available' and invert every assertion. Scaling the oracle would require holding several 64 MiB reservations simultaneously (8 of the 32 permitted), which changes what each case tests rather than rescaling it. So there is no mechanical reconciliation, exactly as E248 suspected and now with the bound named: the design constraint is per-reservation-max 64 MiB vs a bank size that must exceed ~128 MiB for a real session. Two clean options remain, both requiring a maintainer call: (a) keep 128 MiB (verified: unit gate 26/27, host suite green) and give the App's observed-context path a larger *dedicated* budget so a full session fits - the narrowest product fix, since only that path needs the headroom; or (b) move the bank to >=512 MiB and redesign the ~15 affected host cases, which is a test-contract change. ## Compatibility and recovery

This is the breaking plugin-first cutover, not a dual runtime. Recognized legacy
lock rows upgrade only on an explicit writer mutation. Unsupported versions,
unknown fields and unsupported typed facts must fail before publication and
retain the original bytes. SQLite future versions must be rejected before WAL
configuration or writes. Plugin rollback restores content, not revoked grants;
database, plugin and binary rollback are distinct operations. Historical missing
implementations must block execution while preserving supported inspection; they
must not be substituted with a newer plugin. Final migration/backup/upgrade
results remain required before readiness.
The managed Registry static-reason variant is now `PluginRegistryStaticReason.NoStaticReason`;
all callers must migrate from the removed ambiguous `None` variant. No alias or
legacy constructor/runtime fallback is retained.

Unsafe writer ancestors retain the existing `plugin.lock_write_failed` error
classification for Native ENOTDIR/ELOOP rejection. Read-only fence errors keep
their existing classification. The fence still rejects before external plugin
directories are created; no Native path guard or installed SDK is changed (E68).

No checklist is marked complete by this record. Use `Refs #45`, not a closing
reference, while applicable requirements remain unaccepted.
